name: Gradient boosting (LightGBM) on lag + rolling + calendar features for tabular time-series forecasting: M5 Accuracy competition lessons (Makridakis, Spiliotis & Assimakopoulos 2022), 'Forecasting with trees' (Januschowski et al. 2022), Kaggle forecasting review (Bojer & Meldgaard 2021), LightGBM (Ke et al. 2017), plus calibration (Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana 2005) and an event-forecasting analogue (Vestby et al. 2022)
type: method family (peer-reviewed competition-analysis papers + the LightGBM library/paper; not an air-alert study)
url: M5 Accuracy results: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijforecast.2021.11.013 (IJF 38(4):1346-1364; preprint PDF https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/M5_accuracy_competition.pdf ); M5 Uncertainty: https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/intfor/v38y2022i4p1365-1385.html ; Forecasting with trees: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijforecast.2021.10.004 (open PDF https://cdn.amazon.science/17/31/0d99831d4add92e711a56abc75f8/forecasting-with-trees.pdf ); Bojer & Meldgaard: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijforecast.2020.07.007 (arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.07701 ); LightGBM paper: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2017/file/6449f44a102fde848669bdd9eb6b76fa-Paper.pdf ; LightGBM repo: https://github.com/microsoft/LightGBM ; M5 winners' code: https://github.com/Mcompetitions/M5-methods ; top-4% simple direct LightGBM write-up: https://github.com/btrotta/kaggle-m5 ; Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana 2005: https://mlanthology.org/icml/2005/niculescumizil2005icml-predicting ; Vestby et al. 2022: https://www.prio.org/publications/13037 ; Hewamalage et al. (forecast evaluation pitfalls, leakage): https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.10716
year: M5 competition ran Mar-Jun 2020; results paper IJF 2022 (preprint Oct 2020). Forecasting with trees: IJF 2022 (online 2021). Bojer & Meldgaard: IJF 2021. LightGBM: NeurIPS 2017; library latest release v4.7.0 (2026-07-18), repo pushed 2026-10-17. Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana: ICML 2005. Vestby et al.: International Interactions 2022.
authors: Spyros Makridakis, Evangelos Spiliotis, Vassilios Assimakopoulos (M5); Tim Januschowski, Yuyang Wang, Kari Torkkola, Timo Erkkila, Hilaf Hasson, Jan Gasthaus (Amazon Research; Forecasting with trees); Casper Solheim Bojer, Jens Peder Meldgaard (Kaggle review); Guolin Ke, Qi Meng, Thomas Finley, Taifeng Wang, Wei Chen, Weidong Ma, Qiwei Ye, Tie-Yan Liu (LightGBM, Microsoft Research); M5 winner YeonJun In (YJ_STU, a senior undergraduate student in South Korea)
popularity: microsoft/LightGBM: 18,889 GitHub stars (MIT licence, checked 2026-10-17); Mcompetitions/M5-methods: 681 stars; Nixtla/mlforecast (lag-feature GBM tooling): 1,288 stars. M5 competition: 7,092 participants in 5,507 teams from 101 countries. The LightGBM NeurIPS paper is listed by Paper Digest as the No. 6 most influential NeurIPS 2017 paper and has many thousands of citations; the M5 results paper has several hundred to over a thousand citations; exact counts not retrieved [uncertain]
peer_review_status: peer-reviewed (IJF 2021/2022 papers; NeurIPS 2017; ICML 2005; International Interactions 2022). Competition rankings are organiser-verified (the M5 organisers reproduced the top-5 forecasts). Individual Kaggle write-ups (e.g. btrotta/kaggle-m5) are self-reported.
target_type: Not an onset target in the source domain. M5 is a COUNT target (daily unit sales, highly intermittent, many zeros) evaluated as point forecasts (WRMSSE) over a 28-day horizon across 42,840 hierarchical series. The method family transfers directly to a binary onset target by switching the objective to binary log-loss (as our src/model.py already does). Note: the M5 tricks that exploit count structure (Tweedie/Poisson objectives, hierarchy multipliers) have no direct equivalent for our onset label.
target_definition: M5 Accuracy: point forecasts of daily unit sales for the 30,490 product-store series, days 1,942-1,969 (H = 1..28 days), aggregated bottom-up to 12 hierarchy levels (42,840 series); scored by WRMSSE. M5 Uncertainty: 9 quantiles (0.005-0.995) of the same series. Generic GBM framing: y(i, t+h) regressed on features computed at origin t; either direct (one model per horizon or horizon band, lags >= h) or recursive (feed predictions back as lags). For our project the analogous definition is y(t) = 1 if a new alert starts in (t, t+H], H = 1 (or 3), per oblast.
spatial_unit: M5: product x store (10 stores in 3 US states: CA, TX, WI), with category/department/state aggregates. No geography beyond state/store. For our use: oblast (24 units) as a pooled 'global' model with a unit categorical.
at_risk_masking: Not applicable to M5 (count target, every day is 'at risk'). One analogous hygiene step in the top-4% write-up (btrotta): rows before a product's first sale in a store were EXCLUDED from training and from aggregate features, i.e. rows where the series was not yet 'live' were removed rather than treated as zeros. GBM libraries do not mask anything themselves: the at-risk mask (oblast not under alert at t) must be applied upstream, before the rows reach the booster (our project does this in the grid and asserts it in tests).
data_sources: M5: Walmart daily unit sales, 1,941 days of history (29 Jan 2011 - 22 May 2016 for train+validation), 3,049 products, 10 stores, plus calendar (holidays, SNAP days, special events) and weekly sell prices. Validation phase: days 1,914-1,941 with a live public leaderboard (3 Mar - 31 May 2020); test phase: days 1,942-1,969, no leaderboard, ranks revealed 30 Jun 2020. Bojer & Meldgaard review six Kaggle forecasting competitions (e.g. Favorita grocery, Recruit restaurant visitors, Rossmann, Wikipedia traffic).
data_source_variant: Not applicable (retail sales, not air-alert data). The analogue for us: one official source (Vadimkin official_data_en.csv, frozen 2026-09-07) for train/val/test, alerts.in.ua API kept as a separate exploratory regime; never mixed (CLAUDE.md data rules).
preprocessing: M5 winners did little classic preprocessing; the M5 paper lists 'does not depend on data pre-processing and transformations' as a LightGBM advantage (trees are invariant to monotone transforms, handle NaN natively and categorical features natively). Real preprocessing effort went into feature construction: lags of sales, rolling means/std over several windows, price features (relative price, price momentum), calendar/event/SNAP flags, ID categoricals. btrotta excluded pre-first-sale rows and December. For our data the important preprocessing (dedup of 113,845 exact duplicate rows, admin-level union per oblast, D-020 causal 24h standing-alert cap, gap masking) is upstream of the GBM and is unaffected by model choice.
known_label_artefacts: M5-specific artefacts: heavy intermittency (many zero-sales days), out-of-stock zeros that look like zero demand, products entering the assortment late (leading zeros), Christmas store closures. Handling: Tweedie/Poisson objectives for the zero mass (winner: Tweedie negative log-likelihood; 4th place: Tweedie; 5th place: Poisson); excluding leading zeros (btrotta); excluding December or Christmas days. Transfer to our project: the equivalent artefacts (exact duplicate rows, exactly-30-minute durations kept per D-010, standing hromada alerts of 439-604 days handled causally by D-020, the 2026-08-30 to 09-01 recording gap masked per D-013) must be fixed in the label pipeline; a GBM will happily learn any artefact that is predictive (e.g. a feature that encodes a '30-minute naive end' or reads across the gap), so artefact handling matters MORE with flexible learners, not less.
model_family: Gradient-boosted decision trees, predominantly LightGBM (histogram-based GBDT with leaf-wise growth, GOSS sampling and exclusive feature bundling; Ke et al. 2017 report up to 20x faster training than conventional GBDT at nearly the same accuracy). M5 top 5: (1) YJ_STU, equal-weight mean of LightGBM models trained per store (10), per store-category (30) and per store-department (70), each in a recursive and a non-recursive version, 220 models in total, each series forecast as the mean of 6 models; Tweedie loss; NO early stopping; (2) Matthias Anderer, LightGBM per store with calendar/price features only (no past sales), adjusted by multipliers from N-BEATS forecasts at the top 5 aggregation levels, custom asymmetric loss; (3) mf, ensemble of 43 LSTM-based DeepAR-style networks (the only non-GBM top-3 entry); (4) monsaraida, non-recursive LightGBM per store and per forecast week (40 models), Tweedie, no early stopping, no hyperparameter tuning; (5) Alan Lahoud, recursive LightGBM per department, Poisson, early stopping, store-department level multiplier matching the last 28-day mean. Almost all of the top 50 with a known method used recursive and/or non-recursive LightGBM per store/department.
features: Canonical M5 / Kaggle GBM feature set (Makridakis et al. 2022 sec. 4.2; Bojer & Meldgaard 2021; btrotta): (a) LAG features of the target: sales at lags 1..7, 14, 28 etc. (direct models only use lags >= the horizon, e.g. lag 28+ for a single 28-day model, or lags >= h for horizon-specific models; recursive models use short lags fed with their own predictions); (b) ROLLING statistics on lagged values: rolling mean/std/max over 7, 14, 28, 56, 180 days, always computed on data shifted so the window ends at or before the forecast origin; (c) CALENDAR: day of week, week, month, year, holiday/special-event flags, SNAP days (known in advance, so legitimately 'future' covariates); (d) PRICE/exogenous: sell price, relative price vs item mean, price change, promotions (top teams found price features important; Finding 7 'importance of exogenous/explanatory variables'); (e) IDENTIFIERS as categoricals: item, department, category, store, state (cross-learning across series: Finding 3, all top-50 used cross-learning, i.e. pooled 'global' models); (f) recency/zero-run features: days since last sale, length of zero-sales run (3rd place used zero-sales-period features). Mapping to our project: lags/rolling = onsets_last_24h, onsets_last_7d; recency = minutes_since_last_start / minutes_since_last_end (discrete-time hazard duration dependence); calendar = Kyiv hour, weekday; cross-series = neighbors_active_at_t, national_active_count_at_t; identifier = unit_code categorical. These are exactly the features in src/features.py.
external_feature_timing: In M5 the exogenous inputs were either known in advance (calendar, events, SNAP days, announced prices) or lagged, so no publication-lag problem arose; the competition supplied future calendar and price files. For GBM in general, any exogenous series must be aligned at its PUBLICATION time, not its event time (Hewamalage et al. 2022 warn that features computed from the full series leak). For our onset model there are no external features (D-013 skipped Telegram/ISW/weather); if added, they must carry their real publication lag and be ablated against the same time-restricted sample.
ablation_design: M5 paper does not report controlled feature ablations; evidence for feature value is from organiser benchmark comparisons (e.g. ESX with promotions/events was 6% better than ES_td without them; ARIMAX vs ARIMA similar) and from teams' own CV. The winner's selection criterion is the instructive part: candidate models were compared on the SAME last four 28-day rolling windows and judged by BOTH the mean and the standard deviation of error across windows; recursive models were more accurate on average but less stable, so they were combined with non-recursive ones. Our project's improve stage (feature blocks A/B/C compared on the same folds, 'folds improved' count, no block accepted) follows the same pattern.
split_scheme: M5: chronological; train days 1-1,913, public validation 1,914-1,941 (28 days, live leaderboard, max 5 submissions/day), then validation labels released and a blind 28-day test (1,942-1,969); one final submission selected per team. Top-4 teams and most of the top 50 used a private rolling-origin CV over at least the last four 28-day windows (4th place: last five windows; 3rd place: last fourteen windows; 5th place: a random sample of 500 days for validation, which is NOT a time-ordered split). Retraining on all data up to the origin before the final forecast was standard in M5 (teams re-estimated after validation labels were released). For our project, D-021 forbids a refit on train+val after early stopping; weekly refit is only an extra row (D-014).
metrics: M5 Accuracy: WRMSSE (weighted root mean squared scaled error, scaled by the in-sample one-step naive error, weighted by dollar sales, averaged over 12 hierarchy levels). M5 Uncertainty: WSPL (weighted scaled pinball loss over 9 quantiles). Improvements reported as % over the best benchmark (ES_bu, bottom-up exponential smoothing). No probabilistic classification metrics; for a binary onset target the corresponding proper scores are Brier / log loss and Brier skill vs a strong baseline (our D-021 primary metric).
unit_of_metric: M5: weighted average across all 42,840 series and 12 aggregation levels (dollar-weighted), i.e. pooled-with-weights; per-level scores also reported (Table 3). Not applicable to within-unit AUC; our project reports pooled AND mean within-oblast AUC, which matters because a pooled GBM with a unit categorical can earn pooled AUC just by ranking oblasts by base rate.
baseline_strength: Strong and explicit in M5: 24 benchmarks (Naive, seasonal Naive, SES, MA, Croston, SBA, TSB, ADIDA, iMAPA, ES and ARIMA in bottom-up/top-down variants, ESX/ARIMAX, combinations, MLP and RF benchmarks). Of 5,507 teams only 2,666 (48.4%) beat Naive, 1,972 (35.8%) beat seasonal Naive and 415 (7.5%) beat the best benchmark ES_bu with their selected submission; the majority of teams were worse than ES_bu by more than 13%. Only the top 50 beat ES_bu by > 14%, the top 5 by > 20%, the winner by 22.4%. Lesson: a well-chosen simple baseline beats most GBM entries; GBM wins only with careful CV and features. The event-forecasting analogue is sobering: Vestby et al. (2022) gradient boosting for sub-national violence (de-)escalation was marginally WORSE than the ViEWS baseline on MSE. Our own result is consistent: pooled LightGBM Brier skill vs the rolling 14-day recent rate = -0.0101 on the final test (H = 1).
calibration: Not evaluated in M5 Accuracy (point forecasts); M5 Uncertainty evaluated quantile calibration through pinball loss. For binary GBMs: Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana (ICML 2005) found that boosted trees (AdaBoost-style, exponential loss) push probabilities away from 0 and 1 (sigmoid-shaped distortion) and that Platt scaling or isotonic regression fixes this, after which boosted trees gave the best probabilities among the methods compared. Modern LightGBM with objective='binary' directly minimises log loss and is usually much closer to calibrated, but distortion returns with class reweighting (is_unbalance / scale_pos_weight), strong regularisation, or base-rate shift [uncertain: no single primary source quantifies LightGBM's default calibration]. Best practice: check a reliability plot on a time-later validation slice and, if needed, fit Platt/isotonic there only (our D-021 rule: calibrator fitted on validation and applied to the same frozen model, with a pre-registered ECE > 0.02 trigger).
calibration_under_drift: Tree models cannot extrapolate outside the range of the training target/leaf values, so a level or base-rate shift after training shows up as calibration-in-the-large error. The M5 2nd and 5th place teams handled level/trend with EXTERNAL MULTIPLIERS (5th: rescale so each store-department mean matches the previous 28 days; 2nd: multipliers from N-BEATS at upper levels); the organisers list 'beneficial effect of external adjustments' as one of the three new M5 findings. Direct analogue in our project: the post-hoc 'V2 recent-rate offset' variant raised Brier skill from -0.0101 to +0.0172 (weekly refit + offset V4: +0.0203) but LOWERED within-unit AUC (0.6320 -> 0.5897), i.e. the gain came from matching the recent level, not better ranking. These were post-hoc and not the pre-registered headline.
uncertainty_of_gain: M5 reported no confidence intervals on rank differences between top teams; the winner's distinctive step was looking at the standard deviation of errors across four CV windows, a crude stability measure. The large gap between teams' 'best ever' submission and their selected submission (672 vs 415 teams would have beaten ES_bu) shows that single-window validation differences are noisy. No DM test or block bootstrap in the source papers. For our project, the D-013 week-block bootstrap CI on the gain over recent-rate is the appropriate tool; small Brier differences (e.g. blend weight 0.6 vs 0.7 differing by 2.1e-06) are within noise.
regime_coverage: M5 test covered a single 28-day window (May-June 2016) with no regime change; robustness to regime shifts was not tested, and the organisers note that conclusions may not hold for non-retail data. Januschowski et al. emphasise that trees are robust black-box learners but are weak at extrapolating trends. For our air-alert setting, regime shifts (Jan-2025 drone surge, 2025 raion/hromada admin reform, Sep-2026 yellow/red reform) are the main threat to a GBM frozen at 2026-07-27; our new-regime check found Brier skill vs recent rate -0.0323 and mean predicted minus observed -0.0421, i.e. transfer failed.
leakage_handling: GBM-specific leakage sources documented in this literature and in practice: (1) lag/rolling features computed without shifting to the forecast origin (a rolling mean that includes the target period); direct models must use lags >= horizon, otherwise in-sample training rows see values that are not available at forecast time; (2) recursive models evaluated on training data look better than they are (btrotta: forum evidence that the recursive approach was good on the training period 'by coincidence'); (3) features or scalers computed over the full series before splitting (Hewamalage et al. 2022: smoothing, decomposition, normalisation or tsfeatures/catch22-style features on the whole series leak); (4) public-leaderboard tuning (M5 paper: the leaderboard should be used for assessing methods, not for indirect hyperparameter or feature selection); (5) random-day validation (5th place sampled 500 random days) mixes future and past; (6) early stopping on the test window. Trees add one specific risk: they will exploit any feature that encodes future information perfectly (e.g. final alert duration), so truncation tests are essential. Our project addresses all of these: features are causal by construction, a truncation-invariance test covers features, baselines and model predictions, a negative control (final-duration feature, centred window) must be caught, purge at every cut-off (t + H <= cut-off), early stopping on validation only, no refit on train+val.
test_window_hygiene: M5 enforced hygiene structurally: the test labels were hidden, no leaderboard during the test phase, and each team had to SELECT ONE submission before ranks were revealed; the organisers reproduced the top-5 forecasts. They report that many teams picked a worse submission than their best one ('probably due to misleading validation scores'). Lesson: pre-commit one model and score the test once. Our project mirrors this with preregistration hashes and a joint access marker written before any test label is read (reports/final_test_access.json).
headline_results: M5 Accuracy (organiser-verified): winner YJ_STU WRMSSE 0.520, 22.4% better than the best statistical benchmark ES_bu; all top 5 > 20% better; all top 50 > 14% better; all top 50 were ML methods and most used LightGBM; of 5,507 teams only 415 (7.5%) beat ES_bu with their selected submission and only 48.4% beat plain Naive. The organisers note that the advantage over benchmarks was smaller at the lower aggregation levels (winner WRMSSE at level 12, product-store, was 0.884 vs 0.199 at level 1, total). Organisers' summary: three new findings (LightGBM superiority on hierarchical retail sales, benefit of external adjustments, importance of exogenous variables) plus three confirmed ones (combining, cross-learning, cross-validation). Bojer & Meldgaard (6 Kaggle competitions): GBDTs performed strongly, global ensemble models generally beat local single models. Counter-evidence for event targets: Vestby et al. 2022 GBM marginally worse than the ViEWS baseline on MSE. Our project's own measurement: pooled LightGBM (9 features) did NOT beat the rolling 14-day recent-rate baseline on the final test (BSS -0.0101, 13,116 rows, base rate 0.139), though it beat it in Kyiv City (BSS +0.0738) and had within-unit AUC 0.632 vs 0.491 for recent rate. [uncertain: citation-free summary of Bojer & Meldgaard taken from the abstract only]
code_available: Yes. LightGBM: https://github.com/microsoft/LightGBM (MIT, actively maintained, v4.7.0 released 2026-07-18; pinned as lightgbm==4.7.0 in our requirements.txt). M5 winning methods: https://github.com/Mcompetitions/M5-methods (organiser-collected code, last push 2023-04). Simple direct-LightGBM reference: https://github.com/btrotta/kaggle-m5. Lag/rolling feature tooling with origin-aware transforms: https://github.com/Nixtla/mlforecast (Apache-2.0, active). M5 data available on Kaggle (m5-forecasting-accuracy).
takeaways_for_project: 1) Our model choice is the community default: a single pooled ('global', cross-learning) LightGBM with a unit categorical and lag/recency/calendar/spatial features matches M5 Finding 3 and Bojer & Meldgaard; no need to justify a fancier model, and D-013's decision to skip hyperparameter search is consistent with the 4th-place team (no tuning) and btrotta's 'simple features, no magic'. 2) Beating a strong simple baseline is the exception, not the rule: in M5 92.5% of teams lost to ES_bu. Our negative BSS vs the rolling recent rate (-0.0101) is a normal outcome and must be reported honestly as D-021 requires. 3) The main GBM weakness is level/base-rate drift: trees cannot extrapolate. M5's 2nd and 5th place fixed it with multipliers matching recent level; our post-hoc recent-rate offset (V2) is the same idea and produced BSS +0.0172, but it was selected after the test was seen, so it can only be reported as post-hoc and proposed as a pre-registered component for any future model (needs the human's approval as a protocol/scope change). 4) Combining is the most robust gain (M5 Finding 2): the winner averaged 6 models per series; a pre-registered equal-weight blend of the LightGBM and the rolling recent rate (our V5 idea) is the most M5-consistent next step, chosen on validation only. 5) Validate on several rolling windows and look at the spread, not just the mean (winner's mean + std over 4 x 28-day windows); our single 4-week validation slice is thin, so the D-014 weekly refit row and the D-013 week-block bootstrap give the needed stability evidence. 6) Do not use class reweighting (is_unbalance/scale_pos_weight) on the onset label: it distorts probabilities and hurts Brier; keep objective='binary' and check calibration on validation (D-006, D-021). 7) Recursive multi-step is irrelevant at H = 1; for H = 3 use a direct label (y over (t, t+3]) as we do, avoiding recursive error accumulation. 8) External features: M5 Finding 7 says exogenous variables matter, but only when their timing is known; any future Telegram/ISW/launch features must use publication time and a time-fair ablation (D-013 lists them as limitations).
best_practices: ADOPT: (a) one pooled global GBM across units with an ID categorical (cross-learning); (b) causal lag and rolling features shifted to the forecast origin, plus time-since-last-event features; (c) calendar features in local time (known in advance, safe); (d) direct (non-recursive) targets for multi-hour horizons; (e) rolling-origin CV over several recent windows, judging mean AND spread of the error; (f) early stopping on a time-later validation slice only (or a fixed number of rounds as the M5 winner and 4th place did, which avoids overfitting the validation slice); (g) equal-weight combinations of a few diverse models, including a strong simple baseline; (h) explicit level adjustment toward the recent rate if pre-registered; (i) pick ONE final submission before seeing the test and score it once; (j) check calibration with a reliability plot and recalibrate (Platt/isotonic) on validation only. AVOID: (1) rolling/lag features that include the target window or are computed on the full series before splitting; (2) tuning on the test or a public leaderboard (M5: many teams selected a worse submission due to misleading validation); (3) random-day validation splits for time series (5th place used 500 random days); (4) class reweighting when probabilities are the product; (5) reading pooled AUC as skill when the unit categorical alone separates high- and low-rate units (report within-unit AUC); (6) assuming M5 conclusions transfer: M5 is retail counts with a single 28-day regime-free test window, while our onset process has hard regime shifts and a much stronger naive competitor (recent rate); (7) refitting on train+val after early stopping without re-validating the number of rounds (forbidden by D-021).
